opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think evaluation is one of the most interesting open problems right now, partly because it's become a real bottleneck for progress, and partly because it forces you to confront what we actually mean by "understanding" an image.

For a long time in vision, evaluation was relatively clean. You had classification accuracy on ImageNet, mAP for detection, IoU for segmentation. There was a ground-truth label and you checked whether you got it right. Once you move to vision-language models, where the output is open-ended text, or where you're generating images from text, that clean picture falls apart. There are many valid ways to describe an image, and many valid images for a given prompt. So the question shifts from "did you get the right answer?" to "is this a good answer?", which is a much harder thing to measure.

A few things make it especially tricky.

First, benchmarks saturate quickly, and often for the wrong reasons. A model can score well on a visual question answering benchmark by exploiting language priors. It can answer "what color is the banana" with "yellow" without really looking at the image. So a high score doesn't necessarily mean the model is grounded in the visual content. A lot of the interesting work has been designing evaluations that can't be shortcut, where you actually have to look carefully at the pixels.

Second, the fine-grained details matter, and they're exactly what aggregate metrics miss. Counting, spatial relationships, reading text in images, attribute binding: whether the red cube is on top of the blue sphere or the other way around. Models that look impressive in demos often fail on these compositional things, and a single number on a broad benchmark can hide that.

Third, there's a growing reliance on models evaluating models, using a strong VLM or LLM as a judge. That's pragmatic, because human evaluation is expensive and slow, but it creates a circularity. If the judge shares the same blind spots as the model being evaluated, you'll systematically overestimate performance on exactly the cases that matter. Understanding when automated judges agree with careful human judgment, and when they don't, is an open research question in itself.

And finally, there's the question of what we're even optimizing for. Human preference is a reasonable target, but people prefer things that are fluent, confident, and aesthetically pleasing, which isn't the same as accurate or faithful. On the generation side especially, you can get images that people rate highly that don't actually follow the prompt.

So what I find exciting is that evaluation isn't just bookkeeping. It's a research problem that shapes where the field goes. Whatever we measure is what gets improved, so building evaluations that really probe grounding, compositionality, and faithfulness is one of the highest-leverage things we can do right now.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think evaluation is interesting precisely because it's where our intuitions about these models break down the fastest.

With image classification, you had a label and you were either right or wrong. With a vision-language model, you ask it to describe a photo or answer a question about a chart, and there are many valid answers. So the first problem is just: what does "correct" even mean? If the model says there are three people in the frame and there are actually three people plus a reflection in a window, is that wrong? Humans will disagree, and that disagreement is signal, not noise.

The second thing is that the benchmarks saturate much faster than the underlying capability. We've seen this repeatedly. A benchmark comes out, models score poorly, a year later everyone is in the nineties, and yet when you actually use the models you still find them confidently miscounting objects or hallucinating text that isn't in the image. Part of that is contamination, part is that benchmarks tend to probe what's easy to annotate rather than what's actually hard. Spatial reasoning, fine-grained counting, reading dense documents, understanding what's happening across frames in a video. Those are hard to turn into clean multiple-choice questions, so they get underrepresented.

And then there's the question of using models to grade models. It's practical, it scales, and I use it. But you inherit the biases of the judge. If the judge likes longer answers, you'll train toward verbosity. If the judge can't see the image well itself, it can't catch visual hallucinations. So you end up needing to evaluate your evaluator, which is a bit of a recursive problem.

What I find motivating is that this isn't just a measurement problem, it shapes what gets built. The things we can measure are the things that improve. So if the field gets evaluation right, especially for the messy, open-ended, real-world cases, I think the models follow. That's why I'd argue it's one of the highest-leverage open problems right now, even though it's less glamorous than training the next big model.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that, as these models become more general, it becomes much harder to say what it means for them to be good. With a traditional vision task, you might have a fixed set of labels and measure accuracy. With a vision-language model, you can ask an open-ended question about an image, and there may be several perfectly reasonable answers.

Then you have to ask: Did the model actually understand the image? Did it pick up on the detail that matters, or did it produce a plausible answer based on the language alone? A response can sound very convincing and still be wrong about what’s in front of it.

So I think the challenge is designing evaluations that distinguish those cases. Can you change something small in the image and see whether the answer changes appropriately? Can you test whether the model knows when there isn’t enough visual evidence to answer? Those kinds of questions tell us something that a single aggregate benchmark score can miss. And they become especially important when you want to understand whether a model will work in a particular application.

r001.rationale: The response discusses plausible but visually incorrect answers and testing image understanding, but it does not mention mistaking an ordinary image for an illusion because it resembles one.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that these models can do so many different things that it becomes hard to say what it means for one model to be better than another. You can evaluate image captioning or visual question answering, but each benchmark captures a pretty narrow slice of what we want them to understand.

For example, a model might correctly identify the objects in an image but miss the relationship between them. And if it gives a fluent answer, it can be difficult to tell whether it actually used the visual information or relied on patterns in language.

So I think the interesting challenge is designing evaluations that distinguish those capabilities. Can we ask questions where the image really matters? Can we measure whether the model notices a small but meaningful change? And can we do that with questions that allow multiple reasonable answers? That makes evaluation a research problem in its own right.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses evaluation challenges, including whether a model truly uses visual information, but does not say that models may mistake a non-illusion image for an illusion because it resembles one.
